newsitem.title: CHINA: China reins in stock, futures trading.
newsitem.headline: China reins in stock, futures trading.

text.p: Hundreds of branches of finance industry firms across China have been closed or merged in recent months as Beijing forces securities and futures houses and banks to stick to their own businesses, analysts said on Tuesday.

Central authorities had issued a series of rules in the past two years requiring financial institutions to pull money out of markets in which they lack expertise and the process was likely to be completed by the end of this year, they said.
"The central government wants to make financial institutions into independent economic entities which are responsible for their own profit and loss," said one trader with a Chinese futures company.
"They particularly want to prevent state banks, insurance firms and other non-specialised state-owned companies from losing money in the risky stock and futures markets," he added.
"The state has lost huge amounts of money during six years of market experimentation," said a stock analyst with a major Chinese securities house.
"It wants to abandon direct involvement in the markets, leaving them to independent firms."

In the latest move last week, the People's Bank of China, the central bank, ordered all stock offices, except those run by securities firms and trust and investment firms, to close by the end of the year.
The ruling covers all securities subsidiaries run by banks, insurance and other firms.

The four major state-run commercial banks -- the Bank of China, the Agricultural Bank, the Industrial and Commercial Bank and the Construction Bank -- were last year ordered to shut their securities branches or departments.
At the end of 1995, China had more than 1,700 securities firms and branch offices, of which about 1,000 were subsidiaries of the four major banks. Most have by now been wound up or merged.
In early March, Beijing ordered futures trading only to be carried out by futures firms, warning securities houses and brokerages in particular not to meddle in futures.
The government also ordered state enterprises not to speculate in futures unless they have a legitimate need to hedge against raw materials requirements.

In a fever for quick profits in late 1980s and early 1990s when China started to revive the markets, thousands of futures and securities firms were set up, most of them run by state financial institutions including banks and credit cooperatives.
After a couple of years of short-lived prosperity, market depression led to most of them losing money, incurring huge losses on the state, analysts said.

But despite a series of crackdowns in the past two years, Beijing now seems to have decided to allow the futures market to survive, though priority for expansion has been given to the securities market, they said.
Securities authorities have implemented a number of measures aimed at expanding the securities markets and have vowed to continue expanding the markets.
A record number of companies have this year been given approval to list shares on the country's two stock markets in Shanghai and Shenzhen.
